message.content: {"decision":"PROPOSE","observations":["The attempted solution models each correct-count c as producing an integer interval [5c, 30+4c] of achievable scores and searches for the smallest score >80 lying in exactly one such interval.","The interval derivation is correct: with w ranging 0..30-c, s=30+4c-w spans [5c, 30+4c].","The attempted solution's manual overlap scan appears to miss that score 131 is not the first unique value; the scan is error-prone and likely misclassified some earlier score.","A deterministic interval-counting procedure can compute, for each score s, the number of c values whose interval contains s, then select the smallest s>80 with count exactly 1."],"procedure_plan":"Parameterize by total problems N, base score B, correct coefficient A, wrong coefficient W (score s = B + A*c - W*w), and threshold T. For each integer c in 0..N, the achievable scores form the integer interval [B + A*c - W*(N-c), B + A*c] (w from 0 to N-c). For each candidate score s from T+1 upward, count how many c-intervals contain s; the answer is the smallest s with count exactly 1. Implement by iterating s and c directly (or by sweep-line over interval endpoints) and returning the first unique s. Also return the corresponding c and w for verification.","uncertainty":"The main uncertainty is whether the intended reading of 'if her score had been any lower but still over 80, John could not have determined this' matches 'smallest s>80 with a unique c'. Under that reading the interval method is exact; the failure was likely an arithmetic/scan slip rather than a modeling error. If the intended reading differs (e.g., uniqueness must hold for all lower scores simultaneously in a stronger sense), the answer could differ.","invalid_operation":"Manually enumerating scores one by one and eyeballing which intervals contain each score, then concluding 131 is the first unique score after 80. This hand scan is error-prone and apparently skipped or misjudged an earlier score that lies in exactly one interval.","replacement_operation":"Compute, for every score s in a bounded range above the threshold, the exact count of c in 0..N with 5c <= s <= 30+4c (generalized to B+A*c-W*(N-c) <= s <= B+A*c), using a deterministic loop or sweep line, and return the smallest s with count exactly 1 together with its c and w. This replaces fallible manual overlap checking with exhaustive counting.","parameter_schema":{"type":"object","properties":{"total_problems":{"type":"integer","description":"N, total number of problems"},"base_score":{"type":"integer","description":"B, constant added to score"},"correct_coefficient":{"type":"integer","description":"A, points added per correct answer"},"wrong_coefficient":{"type":"integer","description":"W, points subtracted per wrong answer"},"threshold":{"type":"integer","description":"T, score must be strictly greater than this"},"max_score":{"type":"integer","description":"Upper bound on scores to scan"},"require_unique_correct_count":{"type":"boolean","description":"Whether uniqueness of c is required"}},"required":["total_problems","base_score","correct_coefficient","wrong_coefficient","threshold","max_score","require_unique_correct_count"],"additionalProperties":false},"source_parameters":{"total_problems":30,"base_score":30,"correct_coefficient":4,"wrong_coefficient":1,"threshold":80,"max_score":200,"require_unique_correct_count":true}}
